Commentate.question: Output each on-screen caption in real time as it appears.

answers.content: It has been known, for some time, that small particles of matter can exert influences on each other through electrical, magnetic, or chemical effects.
Now, a team of researchers at MIT has found a new kind of long-range interaction between particles that is based entirely on the particles' motions.
By studying magnetic microparticles suspended in water, the team discovered that when a rotating magnetic field is applied, the metal particles would spin, simulating the movement of living cells.
But they do not interact with each other.
Here, those same particles suspended in water are immersed in a dense monolayer of other particles that do not rotate, called "passive particles."
As the active particles spin, in the presence of passive particles, they attract each other and come together.
The original distance between the particles is 15x their size.

This long-ranged interaction in the presence of passive particles could lead to the creation of synthetic, active systems that sense each other for applications in drug delivery and new functional materials.
